t: Seleucus I founded Antioch in 300 BCE, and it was the capital of the Seleucid Empire and then of Roman Syria, where it may have had over 500,000 inhabitants at its peak.
It was a chief centre of early Christianity, the place where the name Christian is said in the New Testament to have first emerged, and the seat of one of the five original patriarchates.
Earthquakes, Persian sacks in 256 and 540, the Crusader and Mamluk wars and a change in trade routes reduced it, and after Baybars took it in 1268 it never recovered its size.
dyk: In 1432 there were only about 300 inhabited houses within the walls of a city that had held, at its peak, perhaps over 500,000 people.
ev: After the Battle of Ancyra, Antioch becomes the main centre of the Seleucid Empire
Antioch passes with Syria to the Roman Republic
A huge earthquake strikes while Trajan is in the city
Khosrow I destroys Antioch and deports its people to Persian Mesopotamia
Byzantine forces capture the city after a siege
The Crusaders take Antioch after a siege of eight months
Baybars captures and razes the city

f.founded: Founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 300 BCE, after his victory at Ipsus in 301 BCE; John Malalas gives 22 May 300 BCE for his sacrifice to Zeus at the site.
f.where: On the left bank of the Orontes, beneath Mount Silpius, in the southwest Amuq plain, in Hatay Province in southern Turkey.
f.known: The Seleucid capital; the capital of Roman Syria; one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire; an early centre of Christianity and one of the five original patriarchates; the suburb of Daphne; the Antioch mosaics; the Crusader Principality of Antioch; repeated earthquakes
f.today: The ancient city lies mostly buried beneath the modern city of Antakya in Hatay Province, Turkey.
